newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-U.S. OPEN COURSE -- LONG AND TEACHEROUS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-U.S. OPEN COURSE -- LONG AND TEACHEROUS.

text.p: Facing the longest and one of the most treacherous courses in U.S. Open history, some of the world's best golfers are already talking about laying up with their second shots on at least one par-4 hole.

Congressional Country Club's 7,213-yard Blue Course, which is hosting an Open for the first time in 33 years, is not only brutishly long, it is also covered with devillish rough and water hazards that had players worrying two days before the championship.
Additionally, the lush, rolling course, which is just 15 miles (24 km) from the White House, is being played at a very challenging par 70.

"This one is a beast," Greg Norman, the world's top-ranked golfer, said on Tuesday morning after only one practice round on the course, which features water on at least four holes and unrelenting rough everywhere.
"There is no break out there," Norman said. "It's 7,200 yards of pure no let-up."

Norman, like many others in the 156-man field, said the key to surviving Congressional is to avoid the thick, 5-inch (13 cm) rough that lines the fairways and surrounds most of the greens -- those that aren't guarded by water.
"The crucial thing this week is to keep the ball in play off the tee," Norman, winner of two British Opens and twice runnerup in U.S. Opens, said.

Norman, who finished in the top 10 in the last three U.S. Opens, including a second at Shinnecock Hills in 1995, cited the sixth hole as an example of just how difficult Congressional has been made to play.
The 475-yard par 4 -- a par 5 for members -- has been singled out by many players as the most dangerous on the course, with a big pond bordering the front and right of the green.
"It is not a generous green and with the water on the right it is probably better to play it as a par 5," said Norman, who is not known for his conservative play.
"I'm in half a mind-set, if I have 220 to the hole, to lay up and pitch it on," he said. "Five will be your worse score -- you'll probably make four more times than you'll make five."
Justin Leonard, who won last week's Kemper Open just down the road, is another player who has said he is considering playing the long sixth as a three-shot hole.
"I can swallow my pride and lay up on a par 4, if that's what the circumstances dictate," Leonard said.
The treacherous sixth is not the Blue Course's only brute, however. There are a total of eight par-4 holes that measure longer than 430 yards -- topped by the 480-yard 17th.

The 17th, Congressional's signature hole, starts with a blind drive to a fairway that tilts left and sweeps down to a green sitting precariously on a peninsula jutting from the shore of a lake that frames the last two holes.
The 17th was the final hole in the last Open at Congressional, in 1964, when Ken Venturi won, surviving stifling heat and the last 36-hole finish in Open history.
This year the Open -- for the first time since 1909 -- concludes on a par-3 hole, a decision not universally applauded when first announced.

Traditionalists, including Venturi, wanted the Open to end on a par 4, as usual, but the U.S. Golf Association stuck to its decision and many players have come around to appreciate at least the novelty of ending the championship on a one-shot hole -- perhaps with a hole in one.
"It's a great finishing hole," said Norman, who was one of its critics -- until he played the little tester, which requires a 190-yard carry over the water to a shallow green.
"I really like the hole. It sets up well. There are some great pin positions," Norman said.
"Even though you got the ball in your hand and have the whole teeing ground to find the best lie and the best angle, you still have to execute the shot."
That's all they ask in the U.S. Open.
